title: Why We Remember Save Points
author: Nate LaClaire
excerpt: Memory, ritual, and the peculiar comfort of knowing a glowing crystal is waiting nearby.
body: A save point is a promise disguised as an object. It says that the journey can pause here, that the player’s time matters, and that progress can survive the machine being switched off.

The earliest games made saving impossible or expensive. Passwords, battery-backed cartridges, and scarce save slots turned persistence into part of the design. We learned rituals around them: checking the icon, waiting for the chime, saving twice just in case.

Today, invisible autosaves are kinder and more convenient. But the old glowing typewriter, campfire, or crystal gave rest a physical shape. It made stopping feel like part of play rather than its interruption.

title: The Arcade as Public Square
author: Nate LaClaire
excerpt: Before online lobbies, play was noisy, local, embodied—and watched.
body: The arcade made play public. Every cabinet was both a private contest and a small stage, surrounded by spectators who learned through watching.
Its architecture shaped a culture: limited turns, visible scores, and the constant possibility that a stranger would step up beside you.

title: What the Character Select Screen Tells Us
author: Maya Chen, guest writer
excerpt: A roster is never just a roster. It is a map of who a game imagines can become powerful.
body: Before the match begins, a character select screen teaches us how to read its world. Portraits, poses, silhouettes, and statistics turn identity into a field of choices.
These screens can invite experimentation, but they also expose a game’s assumptions about bodies, archetypes, and belonging.
